evidence.claim: The Egyptian president is the head of state and head of executive power under article 139 of the constitution.
evidence.title: President of the Republic
evidence.excerpt: The Egyptian president is the head of state and head of executive power under article 139 of the constitution.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official constitutional summary from the Egyptian state information service; the office definition is stable across 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Stable constitutional authority in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s office, but not any specific 2022 action.
contrary_evidence: Constitutional authority alone does not show direct control over every security or nuclear decision.

evidence.title: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UN treaty depositary record with direct ratification entry for Egypt.
evidence.ruler_attribution: A state commitment inherited by and continuing under Sisi’s presidency.
contrary_evidence: Ratification does not itself prove good-faith implementation in 2022.

evidence.claim: Egypt is listed among Annex 2 states for the CTBT with a signature entry but no ratification entry on the status table.
evidence.title: Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty status page
evidence.excerpt: Egypt is listed among Annex 2 states for the CTBT with a signature entry but no ratification entry on the status table.
evidence.source_locator: status lines 87-105 and Egypt row in participant table
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UN depositary status table is authoritative for treaty signature and ratification status.
evidence.period_fit: Current status reflects the fact that Egypt had not ratified the CTBT in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State-level posture during Sisi’s presidency; not evidence of a personal operational nuclear choice.
contrary_evidence: Egypt publicly framed the non-ratification as linked to regional nonproliferation imbalance and universalization problems, not a desire to test nuclear weapons.

evidence.claim: Rosatom said it received permission from an Egyptian regulator to start building Egypt's first nuclear plant at Dabaa.
evidence.title: Rosatom gets green light from Egypt to build Dabaa nuclear plant
evidence.excerpt: Rosatom said it received permission from an Egyptian regulator to start building Egypt's first nuclear plant at Dabaa.
evidence.source_locator: Reuters lede in the syndicated story
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting is strong independent confirmation, though this is a syndication page rather than Reuters-hosted original.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State-level regulatory action under Sisi's government.
contrary_evidence: This confirms permission to build, not safe operation or ruler-level prudence by itself.

evidence.claim: Egypt began construction of the first reactor at El-Dabaa, and the article says the reactors comply with IAEA safety measurements and that ENRRA permitted Rosatom to start construction.
evidence.title: Egypt begins construction of first reactor at El-Dabaa nuclear plant
evidence.excerpt: Egypt began construction of the first reactor at El-Dabaa, and the article says the reactors comply with IAEA safety measurements and that ENRRA permitted Rosatom to start construction.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reputable Egyptian outlet with concrete project and safety details, but still secondary reporting.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Reflects the state project under Sisi, but not a personal nuclear-safety decision by him.
contrary_evidence: The article repeats official assurances on safety rather than independently auditing them.
It reports project launch, not operational safety outcomes.

evidence.claim: Egypt said nuclear-weapon states should fulfill their disarmament obligations and that measures to reduce nuclear risk should not substitute for nuclear disarmament, while reaffirming support for a Middle East nuclear-weapon-free zone.
evidence.title: Egypt's delegate in New York stresses importance of fulfilling obligations on nuclear disarmament
evidence.excerpt: Egypt said nuclear-weapon states should fulfill their disarmament obligations and that measures to reduce nuclear risk should not substitute for nuclear disarmament, while reaffirming support for a Middle East nuclear-weapon-free zone.
evidence.source_locator: article body and quoted mission statement
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct 2022 Egyptian diplomatic statement published by the state information service.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State position during Sisi's presidency; not a personal operational control decision.
contrary_evidence: This is diplomatic advocacy, not evidence that Sisi changed Egypt's own risk posture in a measurable way.

evidence.claim: Egypt said nuclear disarmament is a legal obligation and condemned all nuclear threats, explicit or implicit.
evidence.title: False logic of deterrence elevates role of nuclear weapons in security doctrines, First Committee hears as general debate continues
evidence.excerpt: Egypt said nuclear disarmament is a legal obligation and condemned all nuclear threats, explicit or implicit.
evidence.source_locator: First Committee meeting record, Egypt intervention
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UN meeting coverage gives a contemporaneous record of Egypt's official statement.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State diplomacy under Sisi, not a private or military command action.
contrary_evidence: Rhetorical opposition to threats does not prove equally strong action on safeguards or treaty ratification.

evidence.claim: Egypt, speaking for the New Agenda Coalition, said the draft outcome document failed to restore the balance of article VI obligations and reiterated the legal duty to pursue nuclear disarmament.
evidence.title: Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference Ends without Adopting Substantive Outcome Document Due to Opposition by One Member State
evidence.excerpt: Egypt, speaking for the New Agenda Coalition, said the draft outcome document failed to restore the balance of article VI obligations and reiterated the legal duty to pursue nuclear disarmament.
evidence.source_locator: meeting summary paragraph on Egypt/New Agenda Coalition intervention
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official UN meeting coverage of Egypt's statement during the 2022 NPT review conference.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State line under Sisi, not a direct presidential operational order.
contrary_evidence: The statement is about global treaty politics, not concrete Egyptian implementation.
It does not address whether Egypt improved its own safeguards posture in 2022.

evidence.claim: The UN lists the third session of the Middle East zone conference as scheduled for 14 to 18 November 2022, reflecting the ongoing regional process Egypt supported.
evidence.title: Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction
evidence.excerpt: The UN lists the third session of the Middle East zone conference as scheduled for 14 to 18 November 2022, reflecting the ongoing regional process Egypt supported.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: UN background page for the conference process and its 2022 session schedule.
evidence.period_fit: Exact 2022 fit for the diplomatic process.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Regional posture under Sisi’s government, not an individual weapon-safety decision.
contrary_evidence: A diplomatic process is not the same as successful implementation.
The page does not prove Egypt moved from advocacy to substantive regional breakthrough in 2022.

evidence.claim: Egypt transmitted the Cairo Declaration adopted on the occasion of the signature of the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty and reiterated support for nuclear-weapon-free arrangements.
evidence.title: Letter dated 12 April 1996 from the Permanent Representative of Egypt
evidence.excerpt: Egypt transmitted the Cairo Declaration adopted on the occasion of the signature of the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty and reiterated support for nuclear-weapon-free arrangements.
evidence.source_locator: Cairo Declaration annex and transmittal letter
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary UN record of Egypt's own 1996 diplomatic position.
evidence.period_fit: Inherited baseline rather than 2022 direct conduct, but relevant to attribution.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Historical state posture inherited by later Egyptian governments, including Sisi's.
contrary_evidence: This is historical context, not 2022 evidence of Sisi's own conduct.
A longstanding norm does not itself prove present-day restraint.

unresolved_gaps: No direct evidence of Sisi personally making a 2022 nuclear-safety, command-and-control, or crisis-escalation choice.
Concrete durable-conflict outcomes are thin beyond mediation and de-escalatory posture.
Exact chains of command and the effectiveness of pardon/reform mechanisms remain opaque.
There was no 2022 election, so contestability and transfer-rule evidence remains mostly structural rather than event-based.
Household-level distribution and implementation depth of the reform package are still thin.
Independent 2022 household outcome data are still thin, especially on whether transfers and pensions offset inflation.
There is no direct 2022 asset declaration, audit trail, procurement finding, or court judgment tying Sisi or close family to specific private gain from office.
Direct truthfulness/correction evidence from Sisi's own statements is still thin.
Direct evidence of Sisi's personal steering of tactical adjustments and durable outcome attribution remains limited.
